concepts.def: A natural resource, such as timber or solar energy, that is replenished at a rate comparable to its consumption when managed responsibly.
A finite resource, such as crude oil or metal ore, that forms far more slowly than humans consume it and will eventually run out.
The portion of a resource that has already been discovered and can be extracted economically using current technology and prices.
The total energy required to extract raw materials and then process, manufacture, package and transport a material or product.
An assessment of a product's total environmental impact from raw material extraction through manufacture and use to its final disposal.
Designing products to reduce environmental impact, for example by using fewer materials, less energy, and recyclable or low-impact components.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Resource Management & Sustainable Production — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Resource Management & Sustainable Production brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Resource Management & Sustainable Production.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A renewable resource is one that:
options: Can never be used up no matter how it is managed
Is replenished naturally at a rate comparable to its use, like responsibly managed timber
Is always cheaper than non-renewable alternatives
Exists only in unlimited underground deposits
Only the recyclability of the packaging
Only the energy used in the factory
A product's environmental impact across its whole life, from raw materials to disposal
How long the warranty lasts
The total energy used to extract, process, manufacture and transport a material or product
The electricity a product uses when switched on
The calories needed by the factory workers
The energy released when a product is burned

mcqs.q: In the waste hierarchy, which strategy generally gives the greatest environmental benefit?
options: Recycling materials at end of life
Sending waste to modern landfill
Burning waste for energy recovery
Reducing the amount of material and energy used in the first place

mcqs.q: Is recycling the most environmentally beneficial waste strategy?
options: No - the waste hierarchy puts reduction first: not using the material or energy at all avoids more impact than recycling, which itself consumes energy.
Yes - recycling is always the best option for the environment.
No - landfill is the most beneficial option.
Yes - renewable just means the resource is free of charge.

mcqs.q: Does renewable mean a resource can never run out?
options: Yes - biodegradable materials cannot be made from oil.
Yes - renewable just means the resource is free of charge.
No - renewable resources can still be depleted if harvested faster than they regenerate, as overfishing and deforestation show.
Yes - renewable resources are unlimited by definition.

mcqs.q: If a material is biodegradable, is it automatically environmentally harmless?
options: Yes - biodegradable materials cannot be made from oil.
No - biodegradable materials may need specific conditions to break down, and in oxygen-poor landfill they can persist or release methane, a potent greenhouse gas.
No - landfill is the most beneficial option.
Yes - biodegradable products simply vanish without any impact.
